title: Interpret a groin neck and a partial-wall bowel threat
ownerNote: The ultrasound findings should prompt the player to identify the hernia type.
ownerNoteResolution: The player explicitly chooses a hernia type from raw ultrasound landmarks, together with exploration versus attempted reduction according to the partial-wall findings. All four choices have the same two components.
compositionProposal: Two live scored nodes -> ONE joint scored node, subject to manager acceptance. H1-01 and H1-02 show the same after version for traceability; do not accept or count it twice.
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime answer choices are randomized

before.Presentation: Elliot Reed, a 59-year-old man, returns to the surgery clinic with an intermittent right groin bulge.

items.label: Relation to the common femoral vein

before.Task: Which type of hernia do the ultrasound findings identify in Elliot Reed?

after.Presentation: Elliot Reed, a 59-year-old man, presents to the surgery clinic with a newly tender right groin lump. He still passes stool and has not vomited.

items.label: Sac neck
items.value: Inferior to the inguinal ligament; medial to the common femoral vein.

items.label: Bowel at the neck
items.value: Part of one bowel wall protrudes through the opening. The remaining lumen stays within the abdomen.

items.label: Compression
items.value: The protruding wall remains at the opening.

items.label: Doppler
items.value: No mural signal in the protruding wall. Adjacent bowel has mural signal at the same settings.

after.Task: Which hernia type and hernia-directed intervention fit these findings in Elliot Reed?

before: The neck lies below the inguinal ligament and medial to the common femoral vein, identifying the femoral-canal route.
Direct inguinal anatomy is defined at Hesselbach's triangle medial to the inferior epigastric vessels. The recorded neck instead follows the below-ligament compartment beside the common femoral vein.
An indirect inguinal sac enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. The reported below-ligament neck and venous relationship identify a different route.
after: **KEY:** Femoral hernia; operative exploration

The below-ligament neck medial to the vein identifies the femoral route. The trapped partial wall with absent mural signal raises concern for strangulation despite the patent remaining lumen; emergency operative exploration is appropriate rather than a manual reduction attempt.
Femoral hernia; manual reduction

This identifies the route correctly and applies an intervention appropriate for selected acute nonreducing hernias without suspected strangulation. It overweights stool passage: the reported mural perfusion raises a different concern even while the remaining lumen permits passage.
Indirect inguinal hernia; operative exploration

This recognizes threatened bowel but misclassifies the neck. An indirect inguinal sac enters above the ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels, rather than through the reported compartment.
Indirect inguinal hernia; manual reduction

This combines two plausible misreadings: assigning an inguinal route from a groin lump and treating continued intestinal passage as evidence that a reduction attempt is appropriate. Both the neck compartment and mural findings oppose that combination.

explanation.before: The sac neck's relationship to the ligament and vein identifies a femoral hernia. Direct and indirect inguinal labels refer to different anatomical routes.
explanation.after:
The neck below the inguinal ligament and medial to the vein identifies a femoral hernia.
A trapped portion of bowel wall can lose perfusion while the remaining lumen still permits passage: a Richter-type configuration. Suspected strangulation warrants emergency operative exploration, rather than manual reduction.
The closest error is femoral hernia with manual reduction: stool passage does not establish wall viability. Reduction can be appropriate in selected acute nonreducing hernias without suspected strangulation. This asks the hernia-directed intervention, not the first resuscitation order or repair technique.

inference: Locate the sac neck, rather than infer the type from the surface groin bulge. Then: Interpret perfusion in the trapped partial wall, then choose exploration versus a reduction attempt despite continued passage.
focus: The below-ligament neck medial to the vein selects the anatomical axis. Absent mural signal in the trapped wall, with adjacent bowel detectable at the same settings, raises strangulation concern and selects exploration rather than treating an acute nonreducing hernia as suitable for manual reduction.
whatChanged: Require type plus intervention; balance each type/action component twice. Ultrasound reports observations and never names the type. Replace the two-node scaffold with one joint scored decision and an actual partial-wall threat. No preceding answer or feedback is exposed. Manual reduction is the credible acute alternative when strangulation is not suspected, so the perfusion interpretation matters. All neck, wall, compression and flow information is present in the same node; remove the caregiving sentence. The paired-to-one redesign follows the reviewer suggestion and is a manager proposal.

title: Interpret renal phosphate handling after nutrition restart
ownerNote: Answer choices do not make sense.
ownerNoteResolution: All three options interpret the same renal response with parallel grammar and specificity. No mechanism/test/treatment category mixing.
compositionProposal: One live mechanism node -> one new application node under a materially expanded concept version.
keyOrderNotice: key shown first for review only; runtime answer choices are randomized
beforeRole: Exact captured accepted live node at intake; never modified

before.Presentation: Maya Chen, a 31-year-old woman, is reviewed after a monitored nutrition restart following prolonged poor intake.
before.Task: Which physiological process links carbohydrate reintroduction to Maya Chen's phosphate decline?

after.Presentation: Maya Chen, a 31-year-old woman, returns to the surgery clinic to review results from her nutrition restart after prolonged poor intake. Serum creatinine was stable at sampling.

Exhibit.caption: Simultaneous blood and urine samples, before phosphate replacement (constructed data)

after.Task: Which interpretation of Maya Chen's renal phosphate handling is supported by these results?
Options: **KEY:** Renal phosphate loss is inappropriately high.
Renal phosphate conservation is appropriately increased.
Renal phosphate handling remains unclassifiable here.

before: Carbohydrate reintroduction can increase insulin-associated cellular uptake, moving phosphate from the circulation into cells. This is the feeding-related mechanism being asked about.
This selects removal from the body rather than redistribution into cells. It confuses a different route of phosphate handling with the metabolic response to carbohydrate reintroduction.
This treats the lower serum concentration as reduced transfer from the intestine. It does not identify the insulin-linked redistribution associated with carbohydrate reintroduction.
after: **KEY:** Renal phosphate loss is inappropriately high.

Fractional phosphate excretion is (10 x 1.0)/(1.0 x 20) x 100 = 50%. With concurrent serum phosphate of 1.0 mg/dL, that is inappropriate loss rather than the expected conservation. It does not identify the cause of the renal loss or exclude concurrent redistribution.
Renal phosphate conservation is appropriately increased.

This anchors on nutrition restart and its familiar cellular-shift explanation without testing the renal response. Creatinine-normalized phosphate excretion is 50%, not the low excretion expected during this degree of hypophosphatemia.
Renal phosphate handling remains unclassifiable here.

This assumes a timed urine collection is required before any interpretation. Simultaneous phosphate and creatinine concentrations permit fractional-excretion assessment; the supplied pretreatment samples show inappropriate loss. They do not quantify daily phosphate balance.

explanation.before:
Carbohydrate reintroduction increases insulin-associated phosphate uptake into cells as metabolism shifts toward synthesis.
The renal and intestinal options describe removal or reduced entry, rather than this redistribution.
A phosphate fall by itself does not establish refeeding syndrome.
explanation.after:
Fractional phosphate excretion = (urine phosphate x serum creatinine)/(serum phosphate x urine creatinine) x 100 = (10 x 1)/(1 x 20) x 100 = 50%.
At a low simultaneous serum phosphate, the kidney should conserve phosphate; this result supports a renal-loss component.
Feeding-associated cellular uptake can coexist, but does not account for this renal response. The samples assess current handling, not daily phosphate balance or the specific cause of loss.

inference: Normalize the urine phosphate concentration using the simultaneous serum/urine creatinine and phosphate values; obtain 50% fractional excretion. Then: Interpret that result against the simultaneous low serum phosphate: conservation is expected, so the measured excretion supports a renal-loss component.
focus: The ratio uses ALL FOUR paired concentrations; serum phosphate is simultaneously low and samples precede replacement. Feeding history does not select the correct renal-response interpretation.
whatChanged: Paired raw phosphate/creatinine observations now determine renal handling. The feeding chronology tempts conservation/redistribution but cannot answer the question. Samples are simultaneous and pretreatment, with stable creatinine. Direct permitted methods support the fraction; independent adult hypophosphatemia methods support interpretation. The explanation allows concurrent redistribution and does not diagnose a cause or refeeding syndrome. All three choices are renal-response interpretations. Changing urine phosphate alone reverses the loss/conservation choice; preserve the original coherent-category owner resolution.

options.rationale: Fractional phosphate excretion is (10 x 1.0)/(1.0 x 20) x 100 = 50%. With concurrent serum phosphate of 1.0 mg/dL, that is inappropriate loss rather than the expected conservation. It does not identify the cause of the renal loss or exclude concurrent redistribution.

options.label: Renal phosphate conservation is appropriately increased.
options.rationale: This anchors on nutrition restart and its familiar cellular-shift explanation without testing the renal response. Creatinine-normalized phosphate excretion is 50%, not the low excretion expected during this degree of hypophosphatemia.

options.label: Renal phosphate handling remains unclassifiable here.
options.rationale: This assumes a timed urine collection is required before any interpretation. Simultaneous phosphate and creatinine concentrations permit fractional-excretion assessment; the supplied pretreatment samples show inappropriate loss. They do not quantify daily phosphate balance.

conceptVersion.reason: The old objective recalls insulin-linked cellular uptake. This v2 instead tests interpretation of paired renal-handling data and avoids assigning every postfeeding fall to redistribution. That is a material change, so the old concept/card and live question remain exact.
conceptVersion.historyMigration: None. No old concept or FSRS record is remapped, mutated, merged or deleted.
